We investigate the evolution of binary fractions in star clusters using N-body models of up to 100000 stars. Primordial binary frequencies in these models range from 5% to 50%. Simulations are performed with the NBODY4 code and include a full mass spectrum of stars, stellar evolution, binary evolution and the tidal field of the Galaxy. We find that the overall binary fraction of a cluster almost always remains close to the primordial value, except at late times when a cluster is near dissolution. A critical exception occurs in the central regions where we observe a marked increase in binary fraction with time -- a simulation starting with 100000 stars and 5% binaries reached a core binary frequency as high as 40% at the end of the core-collapse phase (occurring at 16 Gyr with ~20000 stars remaining). Binaries are destroyed in the core by a variety of processes as a cluster evolves, but the combination of mass-segregation and creation of new binaries in exchange interactions produces the observed increase in relative number. We also find that binaries are cycled into and out of cluster cores in a manner that is analogous to convection in stars. For models of 100000 stars we show that the evolution of the core-radius up to the end of the initial phase of core-collapse is not affected by the exact value of the primordial binary frequency (for frequencies of 10% or less). We discuss the ramifications of our results for the likely primordial binary content of globular clusters.

We investigate the evolution of binary fractions in star clusters using N-body models comprising up to 100,000 stars, with primordial binary frequencies ranging from 5% to 50%. The simulations are performed with the NBODY4 code and incorporate a full stellar mass spectrum, stellar evolution, binary evolution, and the tidal field of the Galaxy. We find that the overall binary fraction of a cluster almost invariably remains close to its primordial value, except at late times when the cluster approaches dissolution. Furthermore, we find that binaries are cycled into and out of cluster cores in a manner analogous to convection in stars. For the models of 100,000 stars, we demonstrate that the evolution of the core radius up to the end of the initial core-collapse phase is independent of the precise value of the primordial binary frequency (for frequencies of 10% or less). Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the likely primordial binary content of globular clusters.

# Binary Evolution in Star Clusters: Insights from N-body Modeling

## Overview of the Study

Binary evolution in star clusters was investigated using N-body models comprising up to 100,000 stars. These simulations incorporated primordial binary frequencies ranging from 5% to 50%, allowing for a comprehensive examination of how the initial abundance of binary systems influences cluster dynamics. To ensure realistic modeling, the simulations included a full mass spectrum, detailed prescriptions for both stellar and binary evolution, and the effects of the Galactic tidal field. This combination of factors provided a robust framework for studying the long-term behavior of binary populations within evolving stellar systems.

## Global Binary Fraction

One of the key findings concerns the overall binary fraction of the cluster, which almost always remains close to its primordial value throughout most of the cluster's lifetime. This stability suggests that, on a global scale, the initial binary population is largely preserved. The primary exception occurs at late times, when the cluster approaches dissolution. During this final phase, the binary fraction deviates from its original value as the cluster loses its structural integrity and dynamical processes reshape the surviving stellar population.

## Enhancement of Binaries in Cluster Cores

In contrast to the relatively stable global binary fraction, the central regions of clusters exhibit a marked increase in binary fraction over time. This concentration of binaries in the core is particularly striking in certain simulations. In one notable case, the core binary frequency reached 40% by the end of core-collapse, despite the cluster beginning with a primordial binary frequency of only 5%. This dramatic enhancement highlights the profound differences between the central and outer regions of clusters with respect to binary evolution.

## Mechanisms Driving Core Binary Enhancement

The observed increase in core binaries can be attributed to two complementary processes. First, mass segregation causes the more massive binary systems to sink toward the cluster center over time, concentrating them in the core. Second, new binaries are created through exchange interactions, in which dynamical encounters produce additional binary systems within the dense central environment. 

In addition to these processes, binaries are continuously cycled into and out of the cluster cores in a manner analogous to stellar convection. This dynamical circulation means that the core binary population is not static but is instead subject to ongoing exchange with the surrounding regions, reflecting the complex interplay between dynamical interactions and the spatial distribution of binaries.

## Influence of Primordial Binary Frequency on Core Radius Evolution

Finally, the study examined how the primordial binary frequency affects the evolution of the core radius in the 100,000-star models. The results indicate that, up to the end of the initial core-collapse phase, the evolution of the core radius is unaffected by the exact primordial binary frequency, provided that this frequency is 10% or less. This finding suggests that, within this range, the early dynamical evolution of the cluster core is largely insensitive to the precise initial abundance of binaries, offering a useful simplification for modeling clusters with modest primordial binary populations.

# The Evolution of Binary Fractions in Star Clusters: An N-body Study

## Introduction and Motivation

Binary stars play a fundamental role in the dynamical evolution of stellar clusters. As reservoirs of internal energy, they influence core collapse, cluster expansion, and the overall lifetime of star clusters. Understanding how the population of binary systems changes over time is therefore essential not only for interpreting the present-day structure of globular clusters, but also for reconstructing the conditions under which these ancient stellar systems first formed. A central and long-standing question in this field concerns the relationship between the binary fraction we observe today and the primordial binary content that existed when the cluster was born.

## Methodology

To address this question, we conducted a comprehensive suite of direct N-body simulations modeling star clusters containing up to 100,000 stars. These models spanned a wide range of initial conditions, with primordial binary frequencies varying from 5% to 50%, allowing us to systematically explore how the starting binary population shapes subsequent cluster evolution.

Our simulations incorporated several key physical processes that operate simultaneously within real clusters:

- **Stellar evolution**, which governs the aging, mass loss, and eventual death of individual stars, altering the mass distribution of the cluster over time.
- **Binary evolution**, including the internal processes—such as mass transfer, common envelope phases, and mergers—that transform or destroy binary systems.
- **The Galactic tidal field**, which strips stars from the cluster's outer regions and regulates the escape of both single and binary stars into the surrounding Galaxy.

By tracking these processes together, our models capture the complex interplay between internal dynamics and external environmental influences that determines the fate of the binary population.

## Key Findings

Our primary result is that the **global binary fraction** of a cluster remains remarkably stable throughout its evolution, staying close to its primordial value across the full range of models examined. This overall stability, however, masks significant spatial variations that develop within the cluster.

In particular, the **central regions** of the clusters exhibit a pronounced increase in binary fraction over time. This concentration of binaries toward the cluster core is driven by two complementary mechanisms:

1. **Mass segregation**, whereby the more massive binary systems gradually sink toward the center of the cluster through dynamical friction, preferentially populating the inner regions.
2. **Binary creation through exchange interactions**, in which gravitational encounters between stars in the dense core generate new binary systems, further enhancing the local binary population.

## Implications

These findings carry important consequences for observational studies of globular clusters. Because the binary fraction measured in the central regions of a cluster can substantially exceed the primordial value, direct inference of a cluster's original binary content from present-day central observations may lead to systematic overestimates. Conversely, the near-constancy of the global binary fraction suggests that measurements integrated over the entire cluster provide a more reliable tracer of primordial conditions.

Consequently, careful attention to the radial location of observations is essential when attempting to reconstruct the primordial binary populations of globular clusters. Our results provide a framework for correcting such biases and for more accurately linking the observed properties of present-day clusters to the physical conditions of their formation.

# Primordial Simulations: Unveiling the Birth of Galaxies

## Introduction

The formation of galaxies from the primordial universe represents one of the most profound questions in modern astrophysics. Through sophisticated computer simulations, scientists can now recreate the conditions of the early cosmos and trace how the first galaxies emerged from nearly featureless beginnings.

## The Primordial Universe

In the moments following the Big Bang, the universe was a hot, dense soup of particles. As it expanded and cooled, tiny quantum fluctuations in density became the seeds from which all cosmic structure would eventually grow. These **primordial** variations, though minuscule, provided the gravitational blueprints for the galaxies we observe today.

## The Power of Simulations

Modern **simulations** allow researchers to model billions of years of cosmic evolution in a controlled digital environment. Using powerful supercomputers, scientists input the fundamental laws of physics—gravity, gas dynamics, and radiation—along with the initial conditions of the primordial universe.

Key aspects that simulations help us understand include:

- **Dark matter collapse**: How invisible matter first clustered together to form gravitational wells
- **Gas cooling and accretion**: The process by which hydrogen and helium gathered into dense clouds
- **Star formation**: The ignition of the first stars within primordial gas
- **Structure hierarchy**: How small structures merged to build larger ones over time

## Galaxy Formation

The **galaxy** emerges as the crown jewel of these cosmic processes. Simulations reveal that galaxies formed through a hierarchical process—smaller clumps of matter merged progressively to create the majestic spiral and elliptical structures visible in today's universe.

By comparing simulated galaxies with actual observations from telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope, researchers can validate their models and refine our understanding of cosmic history.

## Conclusion

Primordial simulations bridge the gap between the universe's simple beginnings and its complex present. As computational power continues to grow, these digital laboratories will unlock even deeper insights into how the first galaxies came to illuminate the cosmos.

# Abstract

Binary stars play a fundamental role in the dynamical evolution of globular clusters, serving as energy reservoirs that influence core collapse, cluster longevity, and the production of exotic stellar populations. In this study, we investigate the evolution of binary star fractions in globular clusters using a suite of direct N-body simulations spanning a range of initial conditions, including varying primordial binary fractions (10–50%), cluster masses (10⁴–10⁶ M☉), and initial density profiles. Our simulations, evolved over a Hubble time using a high-precision integrator with self-consistent stellar and binary evolution, track the spatial and temporal changes in binary populations across cluster radii.

We find that the global binary fraction generally decreases over time due to the preferential disruption of soft binaries through dynamical encounters, while hard binaries are retained and centrally concentrated via mass segregation. This produces a pronounced radial gradient, with core binary fractions exceeding those in the outer regions by factors of 2–4 by late times. The rate of binary depletion correlates strongly with initial cluster density, with dense clusters experiencing accelerated destruction of wide binaries. We further demonstrate that dynamically processed binary populations exhibit distinct period and eccentricity distributions that diverge significantly from their primordial states, offering an observable signature of a cluster's dynamical history.

These results provide a framework for interpreting observed binary fractions in Galactic globular clusters and suggest that present-day binary demographics can constrain initial cluster conditions. Our findings have implications for understanding the formation of blue stragglers, X-ray binaries, and other products of binary-mediated dynamical processes.

---

*Keywords:* globular clusters, binary stars, N-body simulations, stellar dynamics, mass segregation

## The Dynamical Evolution of Primordial Binary Populations in Dense Star Clusters During Core Collapse

**Abstract**

We present a suite of direct *N*-body simulations, performed with NBODY4, investigating the evolution of primordial binary populations in star clusters of up to *N* = 100,000 members. Our models span an initial primordial binary fraction of 5%–50%, allowing us to systematically characterize how the abundance and spatial distribution of binaries respond to two-body relaxation and the onset of core collapse. Binary orbital parameters are initialized following log-normal period distributions with thermal eccentricity distributions, and stellar masses are drawn from a standard initial mass function.

We find that the global binary fraction remains approximately conserved over many relaxation times, whereas the *core* binary fraction evolves strongly and non-monotonically. Mass segregation drives binaries—being on average more massive than single stars—toward the cluster center, producing a pronounced enhancement of the central binary fraction that peaks near the epoch of deepest core collapse. During this phase, dynamically hard binaries act as the dominant energy source, arresting collapse and initiating gravothermal oscillations. We quantify the competition between binary formation via three-body encounters, the hardening and disruption of existing binaries through super-elastic encounters, and the ejection of binaries and single stars from the core.

The magnitude of the central binary enhancement and the depth and timing of core collapse depend systematically on the primordial binary fraction: models with lower initial fractions reach deeper collapse and higher central densities before halting, while binary-rich clusters undergo shallower, "binary-supported" collapse at earlier times. We discuss the implications of these results for interpreting the observed radial variation of binary fractions in Galactic globular and open clusters, and for the demographics of dynamically processed binaries, including progenitors of blue stragglers and compact-object systems.

counterfactuals.output:
# Abstract

The evolution of binary star populations in dense stellar clusters represents a critical component in understanding cluster dynamics, stellar interactions, and the long-term structural evolution of these systems. We present results from N-body simulations tracking the spatial and temporal evolution of binary fractions across a range of star cluster environments. Our analysis reveals that binary fractions throughout the bulk of the cluster remain remarkably close to their primordial values over many relaxation times, with limited dynamical processing occurring in the intermediate and outer regions. In striking contrast, the central cluster core exhibits a systematic enhancement in binary fraction, driven by two coupled dynamical mechanisms: mass segregation, which preferentially delivers massive binary systems into the core through dynamical friction, and exchange interactions, which convert single stars into binaries via three-body encounters and modify existing binary populations. We draw a physical analogy between this behavior and convective transport in stellar interiors, wherein the core functions as an active mixing region while the surrounding envelope remains comparatively quiescent and preserves initial conditions. Just as convection efficiently redistributes energy and material within a well-defined stellar core boundary, dynamical processes in the cluster core actively generate and concentrate binaries while leaving the extended halo relatively unaltered. This convective framework provides an intuitive and predictive description of binary segregation, with implications for interpreting observed radial distributions of binaries in globular and open clusters. Our findings suggest that observed central binary enhancements can serve as diagnostic tracers of a cluster's dynamical age and internal processing history, offering observational constraints on the interplay between primordial binary populations and subsequent dynamical evolution.

# Abstract

Binary stars play a fundamental role in the dynamical evolution of globular clusters, serving as an internal energy reservoir that can halt and reverse core collapse. Understanding the initial (primordial) binary population and its subsequent evolution is therefore essential for interpreting the present-day dynamical state of these systems. We investigate the relationship between the primordial binary fraction of globular clusters and the binary frequency observed in their cores after several relaxation times of dynamical evolution. Using a suite of Monte Carlo (or N-body) simulations spanning a range of initial binary fractions, cluster masses, and concentrations, we track the spatial and temporal evolution of the binary population, accounting for mass segregation, binary–single and binary–binary encounters, and the disruption and hardening of binary systems. The core binary fraction thus reflects a competition between these processes and does not, in general, preserve a simple memory of the primordial value. We derive scaling relations connecting the observable present-day core binary frequency to the initial cluster properties and discuss implications for constraining the primordial binary content of Galactic globular clusters from photometric and spectroscopic surveys. Our results provide a framework for using core binary populations as a diagnostic of both the initial conditions and the dynamical age of globular clusters.

# Abstract

We present a suite of direct *N*-body simulations of star clusters designed to explore the coupled effects of stellar evolution, binary evolution, and the external Galactic tidal field on cluster dynamical evolution and the survival of primordial binary populations. Our models follow clusters with initial masses ranging from $10^4$ to $10^6\,M_\odot$ over a Hubble time, incorporating up-to-date single- and binary-star evolution prescriptions, a realistic stellar initial mass function, and a range of primordial binary fractions (from 5% to 100%) with observationally motivated initial period, eccentricity, and mass-ratio distributions. Clusters are evolved on circular and eccentric orbits within a realistic Milky Way potential to assess the sensitivity of internal dynamics to tidal truncation and mass loss across the tidal boundary.

We find that the interplay between mass loss from stellar evolution and tidally driven escape governs the early expansion and subsequent dissolution timescales of the clusters, with the tidal field setting the ultimate limit on cluster lifetime. Dynamical processing of the binary population—through hardening of hard binaries, ionization of soft binaries, and exchange encounters in the dense core—substantially alters the binary fraction and its dependence on clustercentric radius, producing a characteristic radial gradient with binary depletion in the outer regions and enhancement in the core. We show that the present-day binary fraction and period distribution retain a memory of the primordial population that is strongly modulated by the initial cluster density: dense clusters efficiently destroy wide binaries, driving the observed anti-correlation between binary fraction and cluster mass.

Comparing our results to observed binary fractions in Galactic globular clusters, we argue that the low binary fractions inferred for massive clusters are consistent with dynamical destruction of an initially high (∼50%) primordial binary fraction, rather than requiring a low primordial fraction at birth. These findings have important implications for interpreting binary populations as tracers of cluster initial conditions and for predicting the formation rates of dynamically assembled exotic binaries, including blue stragglers, cataclysmic variables, and compact-object binaries. We discuss the limitations imposed by numerical resolution and prescriptions for binary evolution, and outline directions for future models incorporating primordial mass segregation and multiple stellar populations.
